A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AcTOL research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison after matching renumbered and relocated material.

before.justification: v2 reports original imitation-learning results in Franka Kitchen, Metaworld, and Unitree D1 robot experiments, together with ablations, robustness tests, and reward analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds visual-shift evaluations and a robot-demonstration fine-tuning experiment.

M1.justification: Section 5.4 adds an optional adaptation stage: fine-tune the encoders on robot demonstrations using the existing AcTOL objectives, then freeze them for behavior cloning. The architecture, VLO loss, and Brownian-bridge objective remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds five Franka Kitchen test scenarios: one, three, or nine YCB distractor objects, plus marble-hinge and metal-slide texture changes. The original datasets and manipulation tasks remain; the fine-tuning study reuses existing Franka Kitchen task coverage.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain CLIP, R3M, LIV, DecisionNCE, and the AcTOL variant without Brownian-bridge regularization. The new visual-shift study uses the existing DecisionNCE comparator; newly cited adaptation methods are not evaluated as baselines.

E3.justification: The new visual-shift evaluation uses policies trained with 15 demonstrations per task. Section 5.4 introduces encoder fine-tuning on 25 robot demonstrations, five per task, followed by behavior cloning with 15 demonstrations per task. The original evaluation procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds two substantial generalization analyses absent from v2: robustness to unseen visual distractors and textures, and whether robot-domain encoder fine-tuning mitigates the human-to-robot gap. These extend the questions tested beyond the retained Brownian-bridge ablation, hyperparameter sensitivity, linguistic perturbations, and reward case studies.

E5.justification: The existing simulation reporting retains three seeds, two camera views, and uncertainty summaries; real-robot evaluation retains ten trials with a fixed seed. The new checklist supplies no additional statistical procedure or uncertainty definition. New Tables 2 and 4 report point estimates.

E6.justification: Original numerical results and plotted findings are retained. New Table 2 reports performance under five visual shifts, with AcTOL exceeding DecisionNCE despite substantial degradation. Table 4 adds frozen-versus-fine-tuned success rates of 61.8 and 86.4 under different encoder-training conditions, rather than revising the original frozen-encoder results.

T1.justification: The VLO definition, Theorems 1–3, mathematical objectives, and appendix proofs are unchanged after matching notation and numbering. Section 2 clarifies dataset and time-index notation without introducing a substantive mathematical revision.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: ordered and continuous vision-language representations without rigid goal-reaching assumptions, improved manipulation learning, and robustness to linguistic variation. The added experiments support these claims without redefining their core scope.

C2.justification: v2 presents human-to-robot adaptation as a limitation and future direction; v3 interprets its new fine-tuning results as evidence that limited robot supervision can mitigate this gap. It also interprets the visual-shift results as generalization without specialized adaptation. The repetitive/cyclic-action limitation remains in Section 7.

D1.justification: Appendix A omits v2 Appendix 8's instruction to apply logarithmic scaling to the Brownian-bridge variance term; this establishes a documentation deletion, not an implementation change. The abstract replaces a direct code-repository link with a project-page link, and the new checklist states that code accompanies the supplemental material.

R1.justification: v3 adds five references covering robust visual manipulation, YCB objects, H2R, Robotic-CLIP, and human–robot domain discrepancy. These contextualize the new experiments; the original related-work discussion and positioning against goal-reaching pretraining remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 adds Section 5.4, a NeurIPS checklist, and funding acknowledgments; relabels the appendices; and updates author/header text, notation, and conclusion wording. The existing scientific narrative and proof organization are largely retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figure 4 showing visual shifts and Tables 2 and 4 reporting the new experiments. Existing figures and tables are retained with renumbering and localized resizing or relocation, including the robot-results table. The first-page layout also changes.

improvement.justification: The visual-shift tests make generalization limits more explicit, and Section 5.4 empirically tests a fine-tuning remedy that v2 proposed only as future work. These provide a limited overall improvement. Missing uncertainty for the new comparisons and removal of the variance-scaling implementation detail temper the gains.
